title: secret sauce
status_note: In daily use across my projects; five commits in, the lint rules still change weekly.
oneliner: My house design system, with tools that enforce it.
role: I designed the system, drew the Stem 7 pixel font, and built the asset generator and the automated art director.

Social cards come out of the same generator, not out of a template tool.

spec.label: commits
spec.source: git rev-list --count HEAD in the secret-sauce repo

body: This whole portfolio is dressed in it. Secret Sauce is two inks, cobalt and vermilion, on plaster, with vermilion allowed once per surface and no gradients, glows or rounded cards.

A system only holds if something enforces it, so sauce-lint acts as an automated art director that flags a page when it breaks the rules, and sauce make generates cards, banners, splash screens and favicons from the same tokens. Stem 7, a pixel face drawn on the grid of my mark, sets the type.
What I learned: rules written as lint checks survive; rules written as prose get argued with.

title: rack10
status_note: Designed and exported as 61 STLs with a fit coupon; print status is not recorded here.
oneliner: A 10-inch modular rack that prints with no screws.
role: I designed it in OpenSCAD: every part, joint and tolerance coupon.

hero.alt: Render of the assembled 10-inch rack in OpenSCAD

media.alt: Exploded view of the rack parts
media.caption: Exploded view: every part is a parametric OpenSCAD module.

media.alt: Front view of one rack bay
media.caption: One bay from the front, as modelled before slicing.

body: rack10 is a 10-inch modular rack for a home lab, designed for a small 180 mm printer. Every part fits the bed, prints without supports and joins the others with printed joints only: no screws, inserts or magnets.

Levels are 4U and stack; trays slide in at any U on tongues that run in grooves. Dovetail tabs, crossbar necks and bowtie keys lock the walls together, and a fit coupon at four clearances (0.10 to 0.25 mm) sets the tolerance before the real print.
What I learned: design the joint you can test first. The coupon decides the clearance, and every part rebuilds from one parameter.

title: font library
status_note: Sixteen families, all free under the OFL, each with its own specimen page.
oneliner: Sixteen free typefaces I drew in code, from pixel faces to a Didone.
role: I drew every family as code: bitmap sources, line-and-arc skeletons stroked with different pens, and a Didone drawn as Bézier outlines. Then I built the library that shows them.

spec.label: glyphs drawn
spec.source: mapped glyphs per style, summed over every style (foundry/library.py)

body: Stem 7 started as my logo, and y'all fellow divers seemed to like it sooooo… I kept going: two new widths of it, then fifteen families that are not Stem 7 at all.

Most of them share one of two skeletons. Hoop's lines and arcs, stroked with a round pen, give a geometric sans; the same skeleton with octagonal bowls and a broad nib at 38 degrees gives a textura; squeezed, sheared or cut by knife lines it gives the display faces. Pip 57's 5×7 bitmaps give the dot, corridor and stencil faces.

What I learned: a typeface is a construction rule plus a list of exceptions. The rule gets you 90% of the alphabet in an afternoon; the exceptions (a three-cell M, a U whose right stem is thin, a v that pathops silently dropped) are where the week goes.
